scenes.text: This copper wire has been bent into a loop. It didn't snap, and in this circuit, the lamp stays lit. Now remember the salt crystal from two videos ago. Hit it, and it shatters. Both solids are held together by attractions between charges. So why can a metal bend, and still conduct electricity? The answer is in how a metal holds its outer electrons.

In a piece of metal, each atom gives up its outer electrons, which are called valence electrons. They don't go to another atom. They spread out through the whole piece of metal, so they're delocalised, meaning they aren't tied to any one atom. What's left behind are positive ions, called cations, packed in a regular lattice. So a metal is a lattice of cations in a sea of moving electrons. The metallic bond is the attraction between the positive cations and the negative electron sea.

Here's the key feature. In a covalent bond, the shared electrons sit between two particular atoms, so the bond points in one direction. In a metal, every cation is attracted to the electrons all around it, in every direction. The metallic bond has no fixed direction. Chemists call it non-directional, and that's what lets a metal bend.

First, conductivity. A current is a flow of charge, so a conductor needs charged particles that can move. Connect a battery, and the delocalised electrons drift toward the positive terminal, while new electrons flow in from the negative end. The cations stay where they are. They only vibrate. So metals conduct as solids, because their electrons are already free to move. In the salt crystal, the ions are locked in place until it melts or dissolves.

Now hit the metal. The force pushes one layer of cations to slide over the next layer. After the slide, each cation still has the electron sea all around it, so it's still attracted on every side. Nothing has to pull apart. In a salt crystal, the same slide would put positive ions next to positive ions. They'd repel, and the crystal would split. In the metal, the electron sea keeps the attraction going, so the metal changes shape instead of breaking.

That's why metals are malleable, meaning they can be hammered or rolled into sheets, and ductile, meaning they can be drawn into wires. And here's the answer to our question. Bending moves the cations, but it doesn't trap the electrons. The electron sea is still continuous through the bent wire, so it still conducts.

Here's a pattern exam questions love. To conduct, a substance needs charged particles that are free to move. In a metal, those are the delocalised electrons, so it conducts as a solid and as a liquid. In an ionic compound, they're the ions, so it conducts only when molten or dissolved. And in a molecular substance, like sugar or pure water, the outer electrons are held in bonds and lone pairs, so there's almost nothing free to carry the charge.
Quick prediction. Sodium gives one electron per atom to the sea, and magnesium gives two. Which metal would you expect to melt at a higher temperature? Have a think.

Magnesium. Its cations have a charge of plus two, and there are twice as many electrons in the sea for each atom, so the attraction is stronger. Sodium melts at about ninety-eight degrees Celsius, but magnesium melts at about six hundred and fifty. More electrons in the sea, and a higher charge on each cation, make a stronger metallic bond.

Now mix in other atoms. An alloy is a metal mixed with other elements. The gold-coloured Australian coins from the first video in this series are mostly copper, with some aluminium and nickel. Aluminium atoms are bigger than copper atoms, so they sit in the lattice like bumps in the layers. When a layer tries to slide, the bumps get in the way, so it takes more force. The alloy is harder than pure copper, which helps the coins resist wear. But the electron sea is still there, so it still conducts.
So here's a line to keep. Metals slide, salts split. Metal layers slide because the electron sea holds every cation, and ionic crystals split because sliding brings like charges together.
Your turn. Aluminium can be rolled into thin foil, and the foil still conducts electricity. Explain both of these properties, using the structure of aluminium. Pause here to answer.

Aluminium is a lattice of cations in a sea of delocalised electrons. The bonding is non-directional, so layers of cations can slide over each other while the sea keeps them attracted. The electrons are still free to move through the foil, so it conducts. Saying the metallic bonds break when it's rolled is the classic slip.

Last one. Sterling silver is about ninety-two point five percent silver, and seven point five percent copper. It's harder than pure silver. Explain why, in terms of its structure. Pause here to answer.

The copper atoms are a different size from the silver atoms, so they disrupt the regular lattice. When a force is applied, layers can't slide past those spots as easily, so more force is needed to change the shape. Saying it's harder because it contains more atoms is the trap. It's the disrupted layers that matter.

So in metals, delocalised electrons explain both bending and conducting. But metals aren't the only solids with delocalised electrons. The graphite in a pencil conducts too, and it's made only of carbon. Diamond is also pure carbon, yet it's the hardest natural substance, and it doesn't conduct at all. And sand, silicon dioxide, is hard as well. Next time, we'll find out why diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide have such different properties.
